items.title: Names for two thirds
items.question: Which fractions are equivalent to $\tfrac{2}{3}$? Select all that apply.

You doubled the top but tripled the bottom. Both must be multiplied by the same number.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check that the top and the bottom were multiplied by the same number.

explain.text: $\tfrac{4}{6}$, $\tfrac{10}{15}$ and $\tfrac{6}{9}$ multiply top and bottom by 2, 5 and 3. $\tfrac{3}{4}$ adds 1 to both, and $\tfrac{4}{9}$ uses different numbers, so both change the amount.

widget.accept: $\tfrac{1}{12}$, or a decimal that rounds to 0.083.

items.title: Fund payout
items.prose: A fund made £2,400 profit. The manager takes $\tfrac{1}{5}$ of it. The rest is split equally between 3 investors.
items.question: How many pounds does one investor get?

feedback.correct: A third of the £1,920 left after the fee.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take out the manager's fifth, then split what is left 3 ways.

byKey.no-fee: That is a third of the whole profit. The manager's fifth comes out first.
byKey.fee-split: You split the manager's fifth 3 ways. The investors share the other four fifths.
byKey.rest: That is all the investors' money together. Split it 3 ways.
byKey.fee: That is the manager's fifth. The question asks about one investor.

explain.text: After the fee, $\tfrac{4}{5}$ of £2,400 is £1,920. A third of that is £640. As one step, $\tfrac{1}{3} \times \tfrac{4}{5} = \tfrac{4}{15}$, and $\tfrac{4}{15}$ of £2,400 is £640.

widget.label: Two and a half divided by five eighths

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write $2\tfrac{1}{2}$ as $\tfrac{5}{2}$, then turn $\tfrac{5}{8}$ over and multiply.

byKey.times: You multiplied by $\tfrac{5}{8}$. Turn it over: $\tfrac{5}{2} \times \tfrac{8}{5}$.
byKey.upside: You worked out $\tfrac{5}{8} \div 2\tfrac{1}{2}$, the other way round.

explain.text: $2\tfrac{1}{2} = \tfrac{5}{2}$, which is $\tfrac{20}{8}$. Portions of 5 eighths fit into 20 eighths 4 times. The rule agrees: $\tfrac{5}{2} \times \tfrac{8}{5} = \tfrac{40}{10} = 4$.

items.title: Dividing with a common size
items.prose: Here is a second way to divide fractions: give them a common size, then count. Put the lines in order to show that $\tfrac{3}{4} \div \tfrac{3}{8} = 2$.
items.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: Rename $\tfrac{3}{4}$ as $\tfrac{6}{8}$, so both amounts count eighths.
Ask how many portions of 3 eighths fit into 6 eighths.
Six eighths split into groups of 3 eighths gives $6 \div 3 = 2$ groups.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each line needs the one before it.

byKey.ask: The question in eighths needs $\tfrac{3}{4}$ renamed in eighths first.
byKey.count: You counted before the amounts shared a piece size. Rename first.

explain.text: With both amounts in eighths, dividing is counting: 6 eighths hold 2 groups of 3 eighths. Turning over and multiplying gives the same: $\tfrac{3}{4} \times \tfrac{8}{3} = \tfrac{24}{12} = 2$.

items.title: Up a quarter, down a fifth
items.prose: You buy a share for £40. Over a month its price rises by $\tfrac{1}{4}$ of what you paid. The next month it falls by $\tfrac{1}{5}$ of its new price.
items.question: What is your overall profit, in pounds?

widget.label: Overall profit in pounds
widget.accept: £0. The price ends at £40, where it started.

feedback.correct: The fall exactly undoes the rise.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work month by month: find the new price, then the fall from it.

byKey.subtract: You took a fifth of £40, or did $\tfrac{1}{4} - \tfrac{1}{5} = \tfrac{1}{20}$ of £40. The fall is a fifth of £50, not of £40.
byKey.rise-only: That is the profit after the first month. The second month takes a fifth of £50 away.
byKey.loss: You found a loss. The fall is £10 and the rise was £10, so they cancel.

explain.text: A quarter of £40 is £10, so the price rises to £50. A fifth of £50 is £10, so it falls back to £40. A rise of $\tfrac{1}{4}$ and a fall of $\tfrac{1}{5}$ cancel because each fraction is of a different amount.

items.title: Your share of a payout
items.prompt:
You own $\tfrac{3}{4}$ of a small firm. This year it made £900 profit and paid out $\tfrac{2}{3}$ of the profit to its owners.

(a) Describe an area model, in words or a sketch. It should show your share as a fraction of the profit.

(b) Find that fraction and the amount in pounds.

(c) Explain why your fraction is smaller than both $\tfrac{3}{4}$ and $\tfrac{2}{3}$.

(d) Your partner says you get $\tfrac{3}{4} + \tfrac{2}{3}$ of the profit. Explain what is wrong.
items.model:
**(a)** Draw a rectangle for the £900 profit. Cut it into 3 equal rows and shade 2 rows: that is the $\tfrac{2}{3}$ paid out. Cut it into 4 equal columns and hatch 3 columns: that is your $\tfrac{3}{4}$. The rectangle now has $3 \times 4 = 12$ equal pieces, each worth $£900 \div 12 = £75$.

**(b)** Your share is the part that is both paid out and yours: 2 rows of 3 columns, so $2 \times 3 = 6$ pieces. That is $\tfrac{3}{4} \times \tfrac{2}{3} = \tfrac{6}{12} = \tfrac{1}{2}$ of the profit. In pounds, $6 \times £75 = £450$. Check: the payout is $\tfrac{2}{3}$ of £900, which is £600, and $\tfrac{3}{4}$ of £600 is £450.

**(c)** You get a part ($\tfrac{3}{4}$) of a part ($\tfrac{2}{3}$ of the profit). Taking $\tfrac{3}{4}$ of the payout gives less than the whole payout, so your share is less than $\tfrac{2}{3}$. The payout is less than the whole profit, so your $\tfrac{3}{4}$ of it is less than $\tfrac{3}{4}$ of the profit. So $\tfrac{1}{2}$ is below both.

**(d)** $\tfrac{3}{4} + \tfrac{2}{3} = \tfrac{9}{12} + \tfrac{8}{12} = \tfrac{17}{12}$, which is more than the whole profit: £1,275 out of £900. That is impossible. "Your quarter-share of the payout" means $\tfrac{3}{4}$ **of** $\tfrac{2}{3}$, which is multiplying, not adding.

rubric.text: Describes an area model cut one way into thirds and the other way into quarters, giving 12 equal pieces.
Identifies the overlap as 6 of 12 pieces and gives the fraction as $\tfrac{6}{12}$ or $\tfrac{1}{2}$.
Finds £450 with working (£75 per piece, or $\tfrac{3}{4}$ of the £600 payout).
Explains that a part of a part is smaller than each part, giving a reason for each comparison.
Shows the sum is $\tfrac{17}{12}$, more than the whole profit, and says "of" means multiply.

items.title: Smallest first
items.question: Put these fractions in order, smallest first.

feedback.correct: Thirty, thirty-six, forty and forty-five sixtieths.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Rename all four with a common size, such as sixtieths.

byKey.three-quarters: $\tfrac{3}{4}$ is the biggest: it misses only a quarter.

explain.text: In sixtieths the four fractions are 30, 36, 40 and 45. So the order is $\tfrac{1}{2}$, $\tfrac{3}{5}$, $\tfrac{2}{3}$, $\tfrac{3}{4}$.
